questions.question: How do you talk about your projects in an interview?
questions.title: Talking About Your Projects
questions.direct_answer: For each project, prepare a 60-second story: what it is, what YOU did, the stack, one hard part and how you solved it, and the result. Structure it as Context -> Your Role -> Tech -> Challenge -> Solution -> Result. Pick the 1-2 projects you know best (you'll be asked follow-ups), be ready to go deep on any part (why this gem, why this schema, a bug you hit), and be honest about what you'd do differently. Have a deployed link or repo ready. The goal is to show you built real things and can explain your decisions, not to list every feature.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have a 60-second story (Context/Role/Tech/Challenge/Solution/Result) and can go deep on follow-ups.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing every feature instead of your decisions; or picking a project you can't go deep on.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: 60-second story: Context -> Your Role -> Tech -> Challenge -> Solution -> Result. Pick 1-2 you know deep; be ready for follow-ups.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Talking About Your Projects simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: A 60-Second Story For Each Project
sections.content: For each project, prepare a 60-second story: what it is, what YOU did, the stack, one hard part and how you solved it, and the result. Structure it as Context -> Your Role -> Tech -> Challenge -> Solution -> Result. Pick the 1-2 projects you know best, because you'll be asked follow-ups — be ready to go deep on any part (why this gem, why this schema, a bug you hit), and be honest about what you'd do differently. Have a deployed link or repo ready. The goal is to show you built real things and can explain your decisions, not to list every feature, so focus on one or two projects you can defend in depth rather than five you can only describe superficially.

sections.title: Project Story Structure
sections.content:
Context -> Role -> Tech -> Challenge -> Solution -> Result.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[Context: what it is] --> R[Role: what YOU did]
  R --> T[Tech: stack]
  T --> Ch[Challenge]
  Ch --> S[Solution]
  S --> Re[Result]
```

sections.title: Project story outline
sections.content:
```ruby
# 60-second project story outline:

# Context:  'A URL shortener I built to learn Rails and background jobs.'
# Role:    'I built it solo — backend, schema, and the Sidekiq worker.'
# Tech:    'Rails 7, PostgreSQL, Sidekiq + Redis, Devise for auth.'
# Challenge: 'The redirect needed to be fast under load.'
# Solution: 'I cached the short->long mapping in Redis and added an index on the slug.'
# Result:  'Redirects stayed under 10ms at 100 req/s; ~500 users.'

# Follow-ups to expect: 'Why Sidekiq over ActiveJob inline?',
# 'Why Redis for the cache?', 'How did you test the worker?'
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Listing every feature instead of your decisions — the interviewer wants decisions, not a feature dump.
Picking a project you can't go deep on — you'll be asked follow-ups.
No deployed link or repo — have it ready to show it actually runs.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Prepare a 60-second story per project: Context, Role, Tech, Challenge, Solution, Result.
Focus on YOUR decisions and one hard part, not a feature list.
Pick 1-2 projects you can go deep on — expect follow-ups on any part.
Be ready to defend choices (why this gem, schema, cache) and a bug you hit.
Have a deployed link or repo ready; be honest about what you'd do differently.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: For each project, prepare a 60-second story: what it is, what you did, the stack, one hard part and how you solved it, and the result. Structure it as Context, then Your Role, then Tech, then Challenge, then Solution, then Result. Pick the one or two projects you know best, because you'll be asked follow-ups — be ready to go deep on any part, like why this gem, why this schema, a bug you hit, and be honest about what you'd do differently. Have a deployed link or repo ready. The goal is to show you built real things and can explain your decisions, not to list every feature, so focus on one or two projects you can defend in depth rather than five you can only describe superficially. A common mistake is listing every feature instead of your decisions, when the interviewer wants decisions, not a feature dump.

sections.title: Concept explained
sections.content: Walk through the example step by step, then say when this approach is a good fit and what you would test at the boundary.
